YOUNG DOCTORS

By: Ntokozo Miya | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South African youth face numerous challenges but every so often, they overcome the odds in spectacular fashion – as we wrap up Youth Month, we celebrate the country's youngest doctors.

Unique Selling Point:
Helen Joseph Hospital has granted us permission to film inside the facility so that we are able to capture the young Dr Thibela, our main character, in her work environment.


Summary:
In 2021, a year after South Africa went into lockdown, 21-year old Thakgalo Thibela completed her medical degree and became the youngest active female doctor in the country. She donned her scrubs and begann doing her rounds at the Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg.
It has been a year since she took on this huge responsibility and Youth Month is the best time to reflect the year gone by, a year that, because of the pandemic, was hugely demanding for seasoned doctors, let alone a young woman who must first reassure almost all her patients that she knows what she's doing before actually treating them.
This is an interesting conversation to have 2 months after the South African Medical Association stated that 38% of its members are planning to leave the country. Just last month, health minister Joe Phaahla told parliament that there is currently less than 1 doctor to treat 1000 patients in South Africa. Considering the dire situation in the healthcare and medical sector, Dr Thibela has no plans to leave at this stage. She tells us why, and lets us into her world as she continues to study towards specialising as a surgeon.
It's an inspirational story of commitment and is just the feel-good we need – the youth have problems in this country, major problems, but once in a while a story like this comes along and gives hope.

Further information:
We also speak to other young doctors – Dr Decent Mkhombo from Mpumalanga and Dr Tsule from the Eastern Cape – who share their experiences and challenges with us, particularly how they navigate the challenges they face as young people, outside of their professional achievements.

FINAL EDIT SCRIPT – YOUNG DOCTORS

INTRO – NATSOUND – Dr Tsule walking through the door
VO – It’s late evening in Gqeberha, Eastern Cape. Dr Nobuntu Tsule is coming off a 12-hour shift at Livingstone Hospital. It’s been a grueling call.
DR NOBUNTU TSULE – MEDICAL DOCTOR – TSULE PROJECT
In most departments, we exceed the 80 overtime hours. Sometimes we do 102 hours per month due to staff shortages.
VO – After a year on the job, 23-year-old Dr Tsule has adjusted to the demanding schedule.
BREATHER - space with nice music, action..
VO - Amazingly, she jumped two grades in high school and was barely a teenager when she embarked on a six-year medical degree at Walter Sisulu University.
DR NOBUNTU TSULE – MEDICAL DOCTOR
I managed to focus on what I came for, that is my studies, which is outside of these other things like alcohol abuse, and all sorts of things, drugs. I was 22 years old when I graduated.
VO - A significant achievement for someone who had to overcome a disadvantaged background and cope with the loss of her greatest fan.
DR NOBUNTU TSULE – MEDICAL DOCTOR – TSULE NEW PROJECT
My dad passed away on the 31st of December 2020. He always had supported me and always was asking me jokingly even, to say: 'When are you finishing?'
VO - She could have chosen any career, but her heart was set on medicine, despite the many problems in healthcare.
DR NOBUNTU TSULE – MEDICAL DOCTOR – TSULE PROJECT
A patient would be looking at me, especially with this, [gestures to herself and laughs] with this body. And they are like: 'Are you the doctor?' But sometimes they are very much welcoming and they're very much encouraging.
LINK - With less than 1 doctor for every 1 000 patients in South Africa, the workload is enough to scare anyone away from the medical profession, but we found some young doctors who are motivated by the prospect of making a difference.
VO – In Gauteng, another exceptional young achiever chose medicine.
UPSOUND – GRADUATION CEREMONY … let the audio breathe
Thakgalo Thibela, Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery [clapping]
VO - Last year, at the time of her graduation from Wits University at only 21, Dr Thakgalo Thibela was the country’s youngest female doctor.
UPSOUND – CLAIRE GREETING DOCTOR AND NURSES
Hello, ladies. Claire, how are you? Nice to meet you, Doctor.
VO – For young doctors, stepping into severely understaffed state facilities like Johannesburg's Helen Joseph Hospital was made worse by the pandemic.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – MEDICAL DOCTOR
You need to see ten, 20, 50 patients in a day and be able to give each one of those patients your utmost best, and we had a lot of people in my group actually quit medicine because it was just too much for them.
VO – The shift starts at 6am, when the medical team hands over the night’s patients. Ward rounds follow before the real workload starts in the out-patient ward.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – MEDICAL DOCTOR
I was involved in the resusc of a 23-year old, and he didn't make it. And I remember looking at him like; 'Oh my God, you are in my age group.' You just have to learn to not take every patient home with you. It's something I haven't mastered yet, but I'm getting there.
VO - Dr Thibela is still learning how much she’s able to do in a world of endless priorities and straining resources.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – MEDICAL DOCTOR
The recent pandemic, it just made things worse and our mental health is really challenged. I had to start seeing a psychologist myself because I was just not coping.
VISUAL BREATHER TO TAKE US TO DR MKHOMBO
VO – The pandemic wasn’t the only challenge for Mapulaneng Hospital in Bushbuckridge, Mpumalanga. It’s recently faced scrutiny for poor service delivery and a lack of security. And yet it’s here that Dr Decent Mkhombo, this year’s youngest doctor, chose to serve.

Speaking to us from the backseat of a car during a quick lunch break, Dr Mkhombo says, barely three months into his work as a medical officer intern, he's feeling the pressure.
DR DECENT MKHOMBO – MEDICAL DOCTOR
When people come to you as a doctor, you know, they relieve so much of not only the physical ailments, but their socioeconomic ailments as well. And to some degree, there's something you can do to help, which is help them physically. But for the most part, there's nothing you can do about it - that does a lot to a person.
VO - Where young graduates compete for posts in better-equipped urban hospitals, Dr Mkhombo had a different mission after graduating from the University of Limpopo at just 21 years old. < Credit: TEBOGO MAKOLA
DR DECENT MKHOMBO – MEDICAL DOCTOR
I chose to come here because this is my community. This is where I was born and raised and I was trying to give back, you know, the best way I know how.
BREATHER/UPSOUND – PRESIDENT CYRIL RAMAPHOSA – 2017 - re-opening of Cecilia Makiwane Hospital – Credit: YOUTUBE – GOVERNMENTZA for visuals
The opening of the Cecilia Makiwane Hospital, a true state of the art hospiital, should be a great moment of celebration...
VO - It was to the far-flung, and recently revamped, Cecilia Makiwane Hospital, outside East London that Dr Johan Nel chose to come after leaving Wits University. At just 26, he now holds three degrees.
DR JOHAN NEL – MEDICAL DOCTOR
I completed my BSc in 2016. I then did an honours degree in 2017, and then I got into medicine at the University of Witwatersrand in 2018, and I graduated at the end of 2021.
VO – The Cecilia Makiwane Hospital upgrade has seen surrounding facilities send more and more of their patients there - piling the burden on its doctors and resources. < Credit: YOUTUBE – EC HEALTH DEPARTMENT for visuals of Cecilia Makiwane Hospital
DR JOHAN NEL – MEDICAL DOCTOR
It's going to be at least 80 or 100 patients. There's only six of you. It can become a bit overwhelming. When you get to a patient, you feel a bit frustrated where you can't really do something for them because of the limitations of the system or something like that, you kind of just debrief with your friends, you share experiences, and I feel like that's something that helps me get through those not-so-great days.
VO – Dr Nel and Dr Tsule have their sights set on specialist qualifications in cardiology. Before making future plans, Dr Thibela and Dr Mkhombo want to first settle in their current roles.
DR DECENT MKHOMBO – MEDICAL DOCTOR
The pressures of this job, I don't think there's an overstatement of it. Every single complaint you hear is true. You get burnt out. You will ask for leave because of the sheer pressure.
VO - Despite the physical and mental strain of the job, Dr Thibela says helping patients recover makes it all worthwhile. She recalls suturing or stitching a wound on a woman’s leg on her first day on the job.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – MEDICAL DOCTOR
I apologized in the beginning, I'm like: 'I'm so sorry, but I have to do this. Can you please bear with me?' I had only learned suturing the year before. And after we finished, she went to my seniors in ED and she's like: 'She treated me so well, you must give her a promotion,' and I was like: 'Oh, thank you!' [smiles]
VO – The SA Medical Association, which represents about twelve thousand of the country's doctors, warns that nearly forty percent of its members plan to leave the country due to the state of the public health system… and yet, the calling is still being heard by some of the best young minds in the country.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – MEDICAL DOCTOR
Come what may, I will not leave medicine. I don't see myself doing anything else but medicine.
DR NOBUNTU TSULE – MEDICAL DOCTOR – TSULE PROJECT
Our health system is failing. We have a shortage of doctors, especially in the rural areas, so we need more doctors this side than they need doctors overseas. I think I want to stay for a long time.



PROMO 1 – 11 SEC
VO - You'll be forgiven for thinking it's bring-a-child-to-work day at the country's busiest public hospitals but these are the newest, and youngest, members of the healthcare workforce.
PROMO 2 – 21 SEC
VO - Despite countless long-standing problems in healthcare, these youngsters had their hearts set on careers in medicine.
DR NOBUNTU TSULE - Our health system is failing. We have a shortage of doctors, especially in rural areas.
VO – They joined the sector at the worst possible time.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – The recent pandemic, it just made things worse and our mental health is really challenged.
PROMO 3 – 21 SEC
VO – South Africa's youngest doctors say discipline got them through varsity...
DR NOBUNTU TSULE – I managed to focus on my studies, outside of these other things like alcohol abuse.
VO – ...but nothing could have prepared them for the Covid pandemic.
DR THAKGALO THIBELA – I was involved in the resusc of a 23-year old, and he didn't make it.
DR DECENT MKHOMBO - We go through a lot.
